title: The Cross Between Two Criminals
paragraphs:
The Cross Between Two Criminals
The Forgotten Truth Hidden Between Two Men Who Deserved Death—And the Savior Who Offers Life to Everyone
There are moments in history that change nations.
There are moments that change generations.
And then there is the Cross.
Not merely because Jesus died upon it.
But because of who was beside Him.

Three crosses stood on a hill outside Jerusalem. Rome intended them to be symbols of humiliation, fear, and defeat. Yet God transformed them into one of the greatest sermons ever preached without a single pulpit.
One criminal died still holding onto rebellion.
The other died holding onto grace.
Between them hung the Savior of the world.
Nothing about this scene happened by accident.
Everything about it was redemption.
This is not merely the story of two thieves.
It is the story of every human being who has ever lived.
It is your story.
It is mine.
And somewhere between those two criminals, every soul must decide what they will do with Jesus Christ.
The Gospel of Luke records:
"One of the criminals who were hanged railed at Him, saying, 'Are You not the Christ? Save Yourself and us!' But the other rebuked him..." (Luke 23:39–43)
At first glance, we simply see two condemned men.
But Scripture reveals something far deeper.
Matthew and Mark tell us that both criminals initially mocked Jesus (Matthew 27:44; Mark 15:32).
That detail is astonishing.
Both men began the same way.
Both were guilty.
Both were dying.
Both insulted Christ.
Yet only one finished differently.
Grace entered the conversation.
That alone should stop every reader.
No one is beyond repentance while breath remains.
No one is too broken.
No scandal is too great.
No failure is too deep.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The cross demonstrates that redemption is never earned by an improved past but received through faith in the crucified and risen Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 5:8).
The Greek word translated "criminal" is κακοῦργος (kakourgos).
It literally refers to an evildoer, a wrongdoer, one who practices wickedness.
Luke intentionally avoids softening their crimes.
These were not misunderstood men.
They were guilty.
Likewise, Paul reminds us that "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23).
The Bible refuses to separate respectable sinners from scandalous sinners.
Before God's holiness, every heart stands guilty apart from Christ.
This is why the middle cross matters.
Jesus was never simply surrounded by criminals.
He was willingly placing Himself where guilty humanity belonged.
Isaiah had already foretold this centuries earlier:
"He was numbered with the transgressors." (Isaiah 53:12)
The Hebrew word translated "transgressors" is פֹּשְׁעִים (posh'im), describing rebels—those who have deliberately broken covenant with God.
Jesus did not merely die near rebels.
He identified Himself with them.
Not because He shared their guilt.
But because He carried it.
Paul writes with breathtaking clarity:
Notice carefully.
Scripture never says Jesus became sinful.
He remained perfectly holy.
Rather, He bore the judicial penalty our sins deserved.
The innocent stood where the guilty belonged so the guilty could stand where the righteous belong—in God's presence through Christ.
One criminal continued mocking Jesus.
His heart never changed.
His words reveal something profound.
He wanted rescue from suffering.
He did not want rescue from sin.
There is an eternal difference.
Many people seek God only when life hurts.
Few seek Him because they recognize the weight of their own rebellion.
The second criminal experienced something miraculous.
Somewhere between agony and death, conviction pierced his heart.
He rebuked the other man:
"Do you not fear God... we indeed justly... for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds. But this man has done nothing wrong."
This is genuine repentance.
Not self-improvement.
Not religious performance.
Not negotiating with God.
Repentance begins with agreeing with God's verdict about ourselves.
The New Testament uses the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia).
It literally means a change of mind that results in a transformed direction of life.
Repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
It is seeing Christ correctly.
The dying criminal then utters one of the most beautiful prayers ever recorded:
"Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom."
In Greek:
Ἰησοῦ, μνήσθητί μου...
(Iēsou, mnēsthēti mou.)
"Jesus, remember me."
No lengthy prayer.
No religious résumé.
No opportunity to perform good works.
No baptism after this moment.
No chance to repair his reputation.
Only faith.
Only surrender.
Only Christ.
Jesus responds immediately:
"Truly, I say to you, today you will be with Me in Paradise."
The word "today" removes every uncertainty.
Salvation was not postponed.
The promise was immediate.

The word "Paradise" comes from the Greek παράδεισος (paradeisos), ultimately derived from an Old Persian word describing a royal garden. Scripture employs it to depict the blessed presence of God. Jesus was assuring the repentant criminal that fellowship with God would begin that very day.
Notice the order.
Not "today you will enter Paradise."
But "today you will be with Me."
Heaven without Christ would not be heaven.
The greatest gift of salvation is not merely escaping judgment.
It is belonging forever to Jesus.
This scene also fulfills another remarkable truth.
The cross becomes the dividing line of humanity.
One criminal rejects Christ.
One receives Him.
Jesus remains exactly the same.
The difference is not found in the Savior.
The difference is found in the response.
John later summarizes this reality:
"Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life..." (John 3:36)
Even in His dying moments, Jesus was still saving sinners.
His mission never stopped.
His mercy never paused.
His grace never ran out.
That is why this account continues to comfort the dying, humble the proud, and call every generation to faith.
Some have wondered whether this passage teaches that good works do not matter.
Scripture gives a balanced answer.
Good works never earn salvation (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Yet genuine faith produces a transformed life whenever time remains (Ephesians 2:10; James 2:17).
The repentant criminal simply had no earthly time left to demonstrate that transformed life.
His faith was real because it rested entirely upon Christ.
The cross also reminds us that religion cannot save.
One criminal died within arm's reach of Jesus and remained lost.
Physical proximity to Christ is not the same as saving faith.
Church attendance, Christian culture, family heritage, and religious vocabulary cannot substitute for personal trust in the crucified and risen Lord.
The cross demands a response from every heart.

The Church Fathers often reflected on this account with profound pastoral wisdom. One ancient observation captures the balance well: Scripture records one thief being saved so that no repentant sinner will despair, but only one so that no one will presume upon delaying repentance. The call of the Gospel is always today (Hebrews 3:15).
Perhaps the most overlooked detail is where Jesus was positioned.
He was literally between two guilty men.
This is exactly what He still does.
He stands between holy justice and condemned sinners.
He is the only mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5).
The cross was never simply an execution.
It was substitution.
It was reconciliation.
It was victory.
It was love displayed in blood.
The scandal of humanity met the grace of God.
And grace prevailed.
That is why the message of the cross continues to change hearts two thousand years later.
No addiction is beyond Him.
No shame is beyond Him.
No betrayal is beyond Him.
No hidden sin is beyond Him.
No broken past is beyond Him.
Because Jesus Christ still rewrites lives.
He still receives those who come in repentance and faith.
He still forgives completely.
He still restores what sin destroys.
He still welcomes those the world has written off.
The cross between two criminals reminds us that the Gospel is not for people who think they deserve heaven.
It is for people who know they do not—and who discover that Christ has done everything necessary to reconcile them to God.
If this truth has stirred your heart, don't let it end with reading. You never know who may encounter the hope of Christ because you chose to pass His message along.

Your support enables us to continue producing Christ-centered articles, discipleship resources, and Gospel-focused content that points people from scandal to grace. Even more importantly, you become part of helping spread the unchanging Gospel to hearts that desperately need the hope of Jesus Christ.
Before you leave, be honest with yourself.
Which criminal are you becoming?
The one who clung to pride until the very end?
Or the one who discovered that even at the edge of death, the mercy of Jesus was greater than every sin he had ever committed?
Your testimony may encourage someone else who is struggling to believe that God's grace is still available.
The cross was never about giving good people another chance.
It was about giving guilty people a new life.
